result.summary: Cadmus's companions are killed by the dragon of the grove of Mars when they fetch water. Cadmus kills the dragon, and on Pallas's advice sows its teeth, which grow into armed men who slaughter each other until five remain and help him build Thebes.

scenes.title: Chapter Argument
scenes.summary: A short prose summary of the episode: the dragon, its slaying, the sown teeth and the founding of Thebes.

scenes.title: The Dragon Kills the Tyrians
scenes.summary: The companions let down their urns, and the dragon rises and kills them all. Cadmus goes to look for them at midday.
scenes.stakes: The Tyrian companions are killed by the dragon.

scenes.title: Cadmus Slays the Dragon
scenes.summary: Cadmus finds the bodies, vows vengeance and fights the dragon. He finally pins it through the throat to an oak.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus risks death against the huge poisonous dragon.

scenes.title: The Voice and Pallas's Advice
scenes.summary: A voice foretells that Cadmus will become a dragon. Pallas tells him to sow the teeth, and he does.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus is frightened by the prophecy.

scenes.title: The Earth-Born Warriors
scenes.summary: Armed men spring from the ground and slay each other. Five survive, including Echion, and help Cadmus build the city.
scenes.stakes: Cadmus faces a new armed enemy; the warriors fight to the death.

alias_notes.explanation: Pallas, Minerva and Tritonia all name the same goddess.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable simile comparing rising warriors to figures appearing as a theatre curtain lifts.
Ominous prophecy that Cadmus will himself become a serpent.

analysis.text: Founding a city requires violence: Cadmus's act against the sacred dragon brings a prophecy of his own punishment, while the warriors' self-slaughter shows civil strife at Thebes's origin.
The story gave Thebes a mythic origin, with Theban nobles claiming descent from the Sown Men (Spartoi).

legacy.text: The sown dragon's teeth became a proverb for actions that sow future conflict.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's theatre simile reflects the Roman stage curtain, which was lowered into a slot to reveal the stage.

language_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athena) advises Cadmus to sow the teeth; the armed men who spring up are the Sparti, "sown men".
"Tyrian nation" means people from Tyre in Phoenicia, Cadmus's homeland. "Ill-fated steps" signals that entering the grove brings doom.
The serpent dividing the two Bears is the constellation Draco, which winds between Ursa Major and Ursa Minor in the northern sky.
"Phœnicians" is another name for the Tyrians, Cadmus's companions, since Tyre was a Phoenician city.
"Son of Agenor" is a patronymic for Cadmus; Agenor was king of Phoenicia. Shadows are short because it is midday.
"Wonted" means customary or usual: the new wound only adds to his usual fury.
Agenor was king of Phoenicia and Cadmus's father, so 'son of Agenor' is a patronymic way of addressing Cadmus.
Pallas is Minerva (Greek Athena), goddess of wisdom, who often aids heroes. Here she helps Cadmus.
'Painted cones' means crested helmets; 'coverings of heads' is a roundabout way of saying helmets.
'Curtains' refers to the Roman theater curtain, which was lowered into a slot at the stage front and raised at the start of the play.
The 'blood-stained mother' is the Earth, which bore the warriors; they beat her breast as they die.
Tritonia is a title of Pallas (Minerva), perhaps from Lake Triton or the river Triton.
'Sidonian' means from Sidon, a Phoenician city; Cadmus came from Phoenicia, so he is a stranger in Boeotia.

context_notes.text: The fountain of Mars is sacred to the war god, and the dragon is his offspring and guardian. This is why Cadmus later owes penance.
A lion skin was the garment of a hero or warrior, and links Cadmus with heroes like Hercules.
Pinning the dragon to an oak completes the victory, after which Cadmus founds Thebes on the site.
Echion became one of the Spartoi ('sown men'), ancestors of Theban nobility. He later fathered Pentheus with Agave, Cadmus's daughter.
Phœbus is Apollo. His oracle at Delphi told Cadmus to follow a cow and found a city where it lay down; this city became Thebes.

literary_notes.text: Cadmus's vow to avenge his men or die with them shows his loyalty and courage.
The dragon's scales are compared to a coat of mail, making the creature's natural armor like a warrior's.
Comparing the dragon to a rain-swollen torrent conveys its overwhelming force as it flattens the forest.
The oak bends and groans as if suffering, giving the tree feeling in the final blow.
The voice's prophecy anticipates Cadmus's later transformation into a serpent, as the poem's theme of metamorphosis is applied to the hero.
Men are described as a 'crop' that 'grows,' treating the sown teeth as seeds and the warriors as a harvest.
The warriors rising from the earth are compared to figures emerging as a theater curtain is raised, giving a vivid picture of gradual appearance.
The killer dies just as quickly, breathing out air he has only just received. Their brief lives make their violence pointless.
